cases.working_notes: Retain learned residual action tokenization, continuous precision, multimodality, and single-pass inference. Use the standalone-versus-sequence contrast to establish where the real-robot advantage lies, not to claim that faster inference causes higher success or less overfitting. Keep the modified diffusion baseline and fully closed-loop execution explicit. Table 3's conditional/unconditional headings conflict with its method groups; use the unambiguous RTX A4000 timings in Table 7. Figure 4's extracted labels do not reliably identify entropy values, so avoid numerical entropy claims. Preserve the unconditional Image Kitchen and BlockPush exceptions. Trial counts are descriptive, not evidence of statistical significance.
cases.abstract: Multimodal demonstrations require policies that represent alternative behaviors without losing the action precision needed for control. We introduce Vector-Quantized Behavior Transformers (VQ-BeT), which learn discrete latent representations of actions or action chunks rather than clustering actions directly. Residual quantization combines coarse codes with finer corrections, while a continuous offset refines decoded actions. A transformer predicts the codes from observation histories and optional goals, enabling single-pass generation instead of iterative denoising. In simulated manipulation and locomotion, VQ-BeT achieves competitive task performance and captures multiple behavior modes, although diffusion baselines perform better on unconditional Image Kitchen and BlockPush. On a real mobile manipulator, it completes 19 of 30 two-task trials versus 11 of 30 for a modified transformer diffusion policy, despite similar standalone-task success; its final success count is at least three times the baseline's on each of four longer tasks. All policies execute fully closed-loop because receding-horizon control fails on this robot. Mean inference on an RTX A4000 takes 18.06 ms versus 573.49 ms, pairing higher sequence completion with faster action generation.
cases.results: VQ-BeT's real-robot advantage is larger for task sequences than for standalone manipulation. It completes 47 of 50 standalone trials versus 45 of 50 for the modified DiffusionPolicy-T, but 19 of 30 two-task trials versus 11 of 30. Across four longer tasks, each evaluated over ten trials, its final success count is at least three times the baseline's. Thus, similar isolated-task competence does not translate into similar sequence completion. All policies are executed fully closed-loop because receding-horizon control fails on the low-cost mobile manipulator, making per-action inference cost relevant to this comparison. On an RTX A4000, mean inference takes 18.06 ms for VQ-BeT and 573.49 ms for DiffusionPolicy-T. VQ-BeT also closes the fridge and toaster in both possible orders, showing that the sequence-completion advantage accompanies observed behavioral diversity rather than a single fixed task order.

cases.working_notes: Center the revision on a separate imitation policy used in both interaction and TD targets, not on fine-tuning it. Retain actor dropout and the visual critic as co-contributions; proposal ablations support gains beyond dropout. Compare final Hang and earlier Drawer checkpoints at their stated budgets, distinguishing evaluations from training curves. Table I gives early-stop RFT success as 15%, contrary to the prose's 'less than 15%'; use the table. Report 85% versus 65% descriptively, not as a relative 20% increase. Lower baseline scores do not establish deterioration from their own pretrained policies. Manual resets remain an evaluated deployment condition.
cases.abstract: Imitation Bootstrapped Reinforcement Learning (IBRL) uses a standalone imitation policy to guide sparse-reward online learning without constraining the RL actor to reproduce demonstrations. The critic compares imitation and RL action proposals both during interaction and when constructing temporal-difference targets, allowing demonstrated behaviors to aid exploration and value learning through the same action-selection rule. Keeping the policies separate also permits different visual encoders for imitation and RL. Actor dropout regularizes the RL policy, and a shallow vision-transformer critic improves pixel-based learning. IBRL matches regularized fine-tuning on simpler Meta-World tasks but outperforms fine-tuning and demonstration oversampling on harder Robomimic tasks. With 50 demonstrations, it solves pixel-based Square within 500,000 interaction steps while the baselines remain below 60% success. Removing either proposal reduces performance even with actor dropout, supporting contributions beyond regularization alone. On real-robot cloth hanging, 30 demonstrations and 30,000 online steps yield 85% success in 20 evaluations per method, compared with 65% for imitation, 35% for fine-tuning, and 15% for oversampling. Hardware learning uses sparse success rewards and manual resets.
cases.results: On the deformable-object Hang task, IBRL exceeds imitation performance while both demonstration-based RL baselines fall below it. With 30 demonstrations and 30,000 online interaction steps, IBRL achieves 85% success, compared with 65% for behavior cloning (BC), 35% for regularized fine-tuning (RFT), and 15% for demonstration oversampling (RLPD). Each score comes from 20 evaluations per method using the same set of initial conditions. This comparison shows improvement beyond the demonstration-trained policy under the allotted budget, rather than merely preserving its competence. In Drawer, the checkpoint after 10,000 interaction steps, using 30 demonstrations, already achieves 100% success for IBRL versus 15% for RFT and 0% for RLPD over 20 evaluations each. The hardware results therefore support both policy improvement and interaction efficiency with sparse binary rewards, under training conditions that include manual episode resets.
